narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 73% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction as a key factor, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class ranking in your third year of law school was the strongest factor pushing the model toward predicting failure. Being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is substantially lower than the average ranking of accepted students (around 5.8), and this weak performance strongly signaled higher risk of bar exam difficulty. Your first-year ranking in the third decile also contributed to the negative outlook, though less forcefully; it was noticeably below the average of 6.0 among accepted applicants.

Your LSAT score of 36 worked in the opposite direction. While slightly below the accepted average of 37.2, it still provided a modest push toward a more favorable prediction. However, this positive influence was not large enough to overcome the academic ranking concerns.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.8, upper-middle family income, and plan to attend full-time were considered but played smaller roles in the final decision.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Building a stronger record in these areas will help future applications. (218 words)
